newsitem.title: UK: Britain's royals join millions on Internet.
newsitem.headline: Britain's royals join millions on Internet.

text.p: Britain's Queen Elizabeth launched a 150-page royal web site on Thursday, opening a world of crowns, corgis and castles to millions of Internet surfers.

The site's home page shows colour pictures of the Crown Jewels and Buckingham Palace and offers surfers access to a wealth of information about today's monarchy, how it works, its members, its many palaces and the huge royal art collection.

A page listing the members of today's royal family includes Diana, Princess of Wales, who was divorced last year from heir to the throne Prince Charles. But Sarah, Duchess of York, who divorced the Queen's second son Andrew, is not on show.
"The royal web site will, I hope, be an interesting and helpful source of information," the Queen said at the web site launch at a north-west London school.

"I also hope that it will encourage you and others to make full use of the World Wide Web, so that we are able to learn more about each other and communicate more easily with each other," she told children at the school.
It was not clear whether the Queen surfed the Internet herself. One section is called "Your questions answered," and lists 18 frequently asked questions about the monarchy.
"Is the Queen the wealthiest woman in the world?", one asks.
"No," is the short answer. "The Queen's wealth has often been greatly exaggerated."
The Webpage explains that the monarch's palaces, jewellery and other assets must be passed onto her successor and cannot therefore be counted as being part of her personal wealth.
"The Queen's personal income, as for any other individual, is a private matter," it adds.
"Why does the Queen keep corgis?" is another question.
The queen was brought up with two Pembrokeshire corgis named Dookie and Jane and "they became great favourites and the Queen...has been firmly attached to the breed ever since".
The most exotic animal owned by the royal family was a Nubian giraffe, given to George IV in 1827 by the Pasha of Egypt, the site reveals.
Cyberspace enthusiasts eager to find out more about Britain's royal family can find the royal site at http://www.royal.gov.uk
They can leave their names, addresses and comments about the site in a special section, headed with a royal crest.
